# What is linear regression? {#sec-linear-regression-what}

```{r}
#| include: false

library(ggplot2)
library(here)

Plot_theme <- source("functions/plot_theme.R")
Plot_theme <- Plot_theme$value

cell_data <- read.csv(here("project/AnalysisData/Cells_Gfap-Pdgfrb.csv"))
cell_data$DPI <- as.numeric(cell_data$DPI)
```

## Picking up the thread

You've already fit a linear regression. Back in @sec-intro-applied-modeling, we asked whether cerebral ischemia raises GFAP intensity, wrote down $\text{Gfap}_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot \text{Condition}_i + \epsilon_i$, and had both `brms` and `parsnip` hand us numbers for it. Since then you've spent a whole part learning what a posterior actually is and how to interrogate one, and another whole part getting to know `cell_data` inside out: its ranges, its trends over `DPI`, which columns move together and which don't. What you haven't done yet is stop and ask what that equation actually *is*, piece by piece. That's this chapter's entire job: not a new technique, just finally naming the anatomy of the tool you've been holding since @sec-intro-applied-modeling.

::: {style="text-align: center"}
***What's the value of knowing A if I know B?***
:::

That's Richard McElreath's way of putting it, and it's worth sitting with, because it's exactly the question a linear regression answers. Knowing an animal's `Condition` (sham or ischemic) tells you something about its `Gfap_Intensity` that you didn't know before: not everything, but something, and a good model tells you precisely how much. Linear regression is our first, simplest tool for turning "A tells me something about B" into an actual number, with an honest account of how confident that number deserves to be.

## The anatomy of the equation you already ran

Here's the model from @sec-intro-applied-modeling again:

$$
y = \beta_0 + \beta_1x + \epsilon
$$ {#eq-linear-regression-simple}

The first time you saw this, it was already filled in with real variables (`Gfap_Intensity`, `Condition`) and real numbers came out the other end. Let's now take it apart term by term, using that same fit as the running example rather than a fresh, abstract one.

-   $y$ is the [outcome]{style="color:green;"}: the thing you measured and want to explain. In that model, $y$ was `Gfap_Intensity`. Elsewhere in this book it'll be `Tisue_Area`, a cell count, a reaction time, whatever column in your dataset you're trying to account for.

-   $x$ is the [predictor]{style="color:green;"}: the thing you believe moves $y$. There, $x$ was `Condition` (sham or ischemic, coded as $0$ or $1$). It could just as easily be `DPI`, drug dose, or any other column that might explain why $y$ varies from animal to animal.

Both $y$ and $x$ come straight out of your dataset: nothing here is invented, which is exactly why the two EDA parts you just finished weren't a detour. Every distribution you looked at, every trend over `DPI` you spotted, was you getting acquainted with the raw material these two symbols are about to stand in for.

The two coefficients are where the real information lives:

-   $\beta_0$, the [intercept]{style="color:green;"}, is the value of $y$ when $x$ is at its baseline: $y$'s "starting point" before whatever $x$ represents has had any effect. In the GFAP model, `Condition` = 0 meant `SHAM`, so $\beta_0$ was `summary(brms_model)`'s `Intercept` line: the expected GFAP intensity in an animal that never had a stroke. If $x$ is numeric instead of categorical (`DPI`, say), $\beta_0$ is the predicted value of $y$ at $x = 0$: day zero, dose zero, whatever "zero" means for that predictor.

-   $\beta_1$, the [slope]{style="color:green;"}, is how much $y$ moves for a one-unit change in $x$. For a categorical predictor like `Condition`, that "one unit" is simply the jump from one category to the other: $\beta_1$ was the `ConditionMCAO` row in that same `summary()` output, the amount GFAP intensity shifted going from sham to ischemic. For a numeric predictor, $\beta_1$ is the change in $y$ per one-unit increase in $x$: per additional day post-injury, per additional microgram of dose.

-   Finally, $\epsilon$, the [error term]{style="color:green;"}, is everything $\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$ don't capture: measurement noise, animal-to-animal biology you haven't modeled, the wobble @sec-intro-applied-modeling already warned you a fluorescence reading carries. It isn't a defect in the model; it's the model being honest about what it doesn't know. You've actually already seen $\epsilon$'s size reported by name: it's `brms`'s `sigma`, sitting right there in the same `summary()` output as `Intercept` and `ConditionMCAO`.

::: callout-tip
Reading $\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$ off a fitted model is, quite literally, the entire payoff of running one: everything downstream in this book is a more elaborate way of getting an intercept and a slope (or several) out of increasingly interesting data. That pair of numbers is worth more than the [lowest p-value]{style="color:red;"} you'll ever see reported, for reasons @sec-appendix-p-values makes in full; the short version is that a p-value never tells you the size of an effect, and an intercept and a slope always do.
:::

## Seeing the line, not just the numbers

A table of coefficients is honest, but it's also easy to read past. Let's put one on a picture instead, using a relationship you haven't fit yet but have already met in EDA: hemispheric tissue area (`Tisue_Area`) against days post-injury (`DPI`). We're not fitting anything here, just looking at what a line through data actually means before @sec-linear-regression-single-continuous fits one properly.

```{r}
#| label: fig-what_intercept_slope
#| fig-cap: A straight line through tissue area and days post-injury, with intercept and slope marked

ggplot(cell_data, aes(x = DPI, y = Tisue_Area)) +
  geom_point(color = "#0072B2", alpha = 0.5, size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, color = "#D55E00", fill = "#D55E00", alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  labs(x = "Days post-injury (DPI)", y = "Tissue area") +
  Plot_theme
```

The dashed vertical line marks $x = 0$, the day of injury itself. Wherever the orange line crosses it is $\beta_0$: the tissue area a line like this one predicts before any time has passed. The line's downward tilt is $\beta_1$: tissue area lost per additional day post-injury. Everything else (every point that doesn't sit exactly on the line) is $\epsilon$.

One honest caveat before we move on, since @sec-linear-regression-assumptions is about to make a whole chapter out of it: a single straight line across the *entire* `DPI` range is almost certainly the wrong call here, and this figure is illustrative, not a finished analysis. Whether a straight line is actually defensible (and over what range) is exactly the question the next chapter teaches you to ask before you trust one.

## When one predictor isn't enough

Real questions rarely stop at a single predictor. What if you wanted `Condition` and `DPI` together, or wanted to control for one while estimating the other? @eq-linear-regression-simple generalizes directly:

$$
y = \beta_0 + \beta_1x_1 + \beta_2x_2 + \dots + \beta_kx_k + \epsilon
$$ {#eq-linear-regression-multiple}

Nothing conceptually new happens here: $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_k$ are just more predictors, each with its own slope, and $\beta_0$ is still where $y$ sits when every predictor is at its baseline. What *does* change is the interpretation of each $\beta$: it now describes the effect of its predictor while holding the others fixed, letting you isolate one factor's contribution from another's rather than letting them get tangled together. We'll put this to work properly in @sec-linear-regression-multiple, once you've seen assumptions checked and a single-predictor model fit end to end.

It's also worth saying plainly, once, why this book doesn't reach for a t-test or an ANOVA here the way a lot of neuroscience training does: both are special cases of exactly this equation with a categorical predictor, nothing more [@gelman2020]. @sec-intro-applied-modeling already showed you that directly when the sham/MCAO comparison turned out to be a linear regression. There's no separate machinery to learn for "comparing groups"; you already have it.

Two coefficients, an error term, and the question of whether the line they describe deserves your trust: that's next.
